The Goldstripe ponyfish, Karalla daura, is a small, laterally compressed teleost commonly inhabiting coastal waters and estuarine environments across the Indo-West Pacific region. Field surveys and growth curve analyses have characterized its life history, beginning with the embryonic phase. At a stable water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], the incubation period is remarkably brief, with the fertilised eggs undergoing rapid development and hatching after just 4 days [ab = 4 days]. The resultant yolk-sac larva emerges from the chorion at a dry weight of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], a minuscule mass that reflects the small egg diameter typical of the family Leiognathidae. This lecithotrophic stage depends entirely on endogenous yolk reserves, and the transition to first exogenous feeding follows shortly after the mouth opens, as the prolarva begins to search for microzooplankton in the plankton-rich water column.

As the pelagic larvae grow and develop through the flexion and postflexion stages, they undergo a pronounced allometric shift during larval metamorphosis, culminating in benthic settlement. Following this transformation, the post-metamorphic juveniles feed actively on small crustaceans and begin a period of sustained somatic growth. At the same ambient temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], data from captive-rearing studies indicate that these young fish attain puberty and the onset of gametogenesis when they reach a total length of 10 cm [Lp = 10 cm], which corresponds to a wet weight of 25 grams [Wwp = 25 grams]. This size at sexual maturation is relatively modest compared to other inshore leiognathids, suggesting an early commitment to reproductive effort that may be an adaptation to variable recruitment conditions in shallow coastal habitats.

Upon reaching reproductive maturity, adult Goldstripe ponyfish engage in iteroparous spawning events throughout the warmer months. The maximum reproductive output for this species has been characterized under controlled thermal conditions at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. Gravid females produce approximately 27 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 27 eggs per spawning event], and they may complete roughly 365 spawning events per year [F_R_i = roughly 365 spawning events per year]. This moderate fecundity per event, combined with a nearly daily breeding cycle, positions Karalla daura as a relatively low-output iteroparous strategist compared to small clupeiform fishes, although the temporal spread of reproductive effort across multiple seasons likely enhances offspring survival in unpredictably productive environments.

Growth continues steadily after the onset of reproduction, and the species exhibits a well-defined asymptotic body size. The ultimate total length recorded for Karalla daura from extensive field collections is 18.2 cm [Li = 18.2 cm], a value that represents the maximum standard length attained by this fish. Derived from length-weight regressions, the corresponding ultimate wet weight reaches 151.4 grams [Wwi = 151.4 grams], a mass that reflects the relatively deep-bodied morphology typical of ponyfishes. This asymptotic size is reached after several years of feeding on benthic invertebrates, and it is generally accompanied by a slowing of annual growth increments as individuals approach their maximum structural dimensions. Such size trajectories are consistent with the family’s general life-history pattern, where adult body size is closely linked to gape-limited feeding on small epifauna.

Longevity data for Karalla daura come from otolith-based age readings and mark-recapture studies, which reveal a moderately extended lifespan for a fish of this body size. Under the stable thermal regime of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C] that characterizes its tropical home range, the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years]. This duration places the species in an intermediate position among coastal leiognathids, whose longevities typically range from 3 to 8 years. The combination of early maturation at a small size, modest fecundity, and a moderately extended reproductive window suggests a life-history strategy that balances the risks of high juvenile mortality against the advantages of repeated spawning across several breeding seasons.
